# On the Peculiar Comfort of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about why I find such peace in unfinished projects. There's a canvas in my apartment that's been half-painted for three months. A novel manuscript sits at 60,000 words, abandoned mid-chapter. In my kitchen cabinet, there's a jar of sourdough starter I've neglected so thoroughly it's probably developed sentience by now. And yet, none of this bothers me the way I feel like it should.

Society tells us that completion is everything. We celebrate the finished product, the polished presentation, the delivered result. Our economy runs on deliverables. Our social media feeds showcase final forms. We take pride in crossing items off lists, in achieving closure, in reaching the end. There's something deeply satisfying about finishing something—I won't deny that. The moment you type the final word of a project, when you step back and see the whole thing, complete and bounded, there's a sense of accomplishment that's genuinely beautiful.

But I think we've made a mistake by venerating completion quite so much. We've forgotten something important about the beauty of things that haven't been finished yet.

When something is incomplete, it's still full of possibility. That's not meant as some motivational poster nonsense—I mean it practically and philosophically. An unfinished painting contains, within itself, every version it might become. The abandoned novel holds within its pages dozens of endings it might have taken. That sourdough starter, given time and attention, could become anything from the most transcendent bread to an educational lesson in mold taxonomy. As long as something isn't finished, it maintains a kind of quantum superposition of potentials.

There's something almost sacred about that state. It's why I think we're drawn to works that feel incomplete—not through failure, but through artistic choice. The fragmented poems of the ancient Greek lyricists aren't worse for having missing sections. If anything, there's something achingly beautiful about reading Sappho's ninth poem and encountering those brackets of lost lines. We imagine them. We participate in the completion, however unconsciously. The work becomes a conversation between the artist and the audience, not a monologue.

When I think of the projects I've actually finished and then never touched again, I'm struck by how final they feel. Done. Over. Historical. Sometimes I'm proud of them, but there's also a peculiar deadness to them. They've been pushed out into the world or into my filing system, and now they just sit there, inert. They're not evolving. They're not calling to me. I'm not learning from them anymore.

The incomplete projects, though—those are alive. Every time I walk past that half-painted canvas, I'm considering it. I'm thinking about what it might become, why I set it aside, whether I still care about the vision I had for it. Sometimes I adjust that vision. Sometimes I realize I was wrong about where it should go. The incompleteness is generative. It keeps creating new thoughts, new possibilities.

I wonder if this is what draws people to ongoing series and long-running shows and extended fictional universes. A truly complete story, perfectly told and definitively ended, is almost melancholic. It's beautiful, yes, but there's also finality and a kind of loss. You can never return to that world with fresh eyes because everything about it is settled. But a story that continues, that sprawls, that keeps generating new chapters and mysteries and character development—that offers something else. It offers a kind of permanent presence. It's always happening, always becoming.

This might explain why we often feel more attached to unfinished series than finished ones, even when the unfinished ones frustrate us. We joke about Game of Thrones fans pining for George R.R. Martin to finish the books, but there's real pathos in that longing. Part of what we're grieving when a beloved series ends unsatisfyingly isn't just the bad ending—it's the loss of the open future. We can't inhabit that world anymore in quite the same way.

But there's a practical cost to loving incomplete things, and I don't want to be naive about that. Incompleteness can be procrastination in disguise. It can be a form of perfectionism—the belief that as long as something isn't finished, I can't be judged for it being imperfect. As long as it's still "a work in progress," any flaws are excusable. They're not the final form. They're not what I'm really capable of. This is poisonous thinking, actually, because it means I'm using incompleteness as a shield rather than approaching it as a genuine state of being.

There's also something to be said for the relief of completion. Not everything should remain unfinished. Some things are meant to be delivered, shared, released into the world. The process of refinement and polish that leads to completion has its own value. There's actually something freeing about finishing something and knowing it's done, even if it's not perfect. You can move on. You can start something new without the weight of the old project hanging over you.

I think the truth is that there should be a balance, and we've gotten the ratio wrong. We should have some completed projects that we're proud of, that we've pushed to a genuine finish line. But we should also have more permission—both from society and from ourselves—to maintain a portfolio of incomplete things. Not as failures, but as ongoing concerns, living documents, permanent works in progress.

This applies to life itself, I think. We're sold the idea that life should have an arc, a narrative structure, a clear progression toward a goal. Childhood, education, career building, family formation, retirement, legacy. A complete story from beginning to end. And while there's certainly meaning in that arc, there's something constraining about it too. It suggests that you're supposed to arrive somewhere, to be finished, to have figured yourself out.

The most interesting people I know are those who've given themselves permission to remain works in progress. They're not waiting for some final version of themselves that will click into place when they've succeeded enough or tried hard enough. They're living inside the incompleteness, using it as a place to experiment and grow and change. They're okay with contradictions because they're still becoming, still unresolved.

The older I get, the more comfortable I am with this. There's a relief in realizing that you don't need to have it all figured out, that the finished version of you—the one who's made all the right choices and understands everything—probably isn't coming, and that's okay. That version might be less interesting anyway.

I think this is why creative work is so important to me—not just for the completion (though that matters too) but for the process of incompleteness. When I'm in the middle of a project, I'm not exactly anyone yet. I'm still deciding. I'm still learning what the project wants to be, and in learning that, I'm also learning something about myself. The incompleteness isn't a shortcoming. It's the actual substance of the work.

There's also something democratizing about incomplete work. A finished piece of art sits in judgment of you. Did it work? Is it good? Can you explain why you made it? With an incomplete piece, there's no need to defend it yet. You can work in the margins. You can experiment. You can fail without it mattering too much. The very fact that it's unfinished gives you permission to not have all the answers.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately because we live in an age of constant completion anxiety. Social media demands finished content. The gig economy wants deliverables. Even our hobbies have been gamified to require completion—achievement systems, completion percentages, "finish" states. There's nowhere left for things to just exist in a state of becoming.

But incompleteness is actually a very old and honorable state. Medieval manuscripts were left unfinished. Composers left sketches and fragments. Sculptors abandoned works mid-carving (sometimes deliberately, to show the marble beneath). These weren't seen as failures. They were understood as part of the artistic process, as windows into the artist's thinking. There was a kind of honesty in showing the work in its unfinished state.

Maybe what I'm really arguing for is the value of process over product, but that sounds too neat and resolved. It's not that process is superior to product. It's that the space between them—the incompleteness—is where the actual interesting stuff lives. It's where you figure out what you think. It's where growth happens. It's where you remain open to possibilities.

I'm not going to finish that canvas anytime soon, I think. And I'm making peace with that. Maybe someday I will. Or maybe it will sit there forever, half-painted, a reminder that not everything needs to be resolved. That beauty isn't only in completion. That the unfinished question is sometimes more valuable than the finished answer.

There's wisdom in staying in the work, in refusing to rush toward the end, in accepting that some things we touch will remain in our lives as works in progress. Perhaps that's not a failure of discipline. Perhaps it's a kind of courage—the willingness to exist in incompleteness, to stay in the middle of something, to resist the false comfort of closure.

In the half-light of unfinished things, we remain alive to possibility. And maybe that's worth something too.
